1.  Pulsed Neutron eXtreme Mechanical Integrity
 Log
A Pulsed Neutron eXtreme (PNX) mechanical integrity inspection log was run to evaluate well integrity and formation carbon
dioxide (CO2) saturation in CCS1 on 6 March 2019. PNX is a pulsed neutron capture tool that is capable of making several
different measurements sensitive to CO2 in the formation and in the casing-formation annulus. Therefore, the PNX can be used to
monitor the formation fluids as well as identify mechanical integrity problems that may allow the CO2 to migrate up the casing
annuli. The PNX was run in the Gas-Sigma-Hydrogen Index (GSH) mode from 7,124 to 200 feet (ft) in CCS1. An evaluation
incorporating the PNX data with the openhole logging was made for the current formation fluids and PNX data inspected for any
annulus CO2 and/or gas. For mechanical integrity monitoring, the PNX is most effective when used as a time-lapse measurement
comparing a base pass to subsequent monitoring passes. Baseline Sigma, prior to CO2 injection, was provided using the
Reservoir Saturation Tool (RST) on March and September 2011. Subsequent RST monitor passes were March, July and
November 2012, July 2013 and December 2014. PNX is the latest generation pulsed neutron tool and was logged in addition to
the RST on 20 July 2014. PNX monitoring passes were acquired in the CCS1 well on 25 October 2016, 8 May 2018 and the most
recent 6 March 2019.

2.  Analysis of PNX Data and Interpretation
The March 2019 mechanical integrity monitoring for CCS1 utilized the PNX. The PNX is the latest generation pulsed neutron tool
and has been optimized for gas, sigma, and neutron porosity measurements in terms of both accuracy and precision. The PNX
introduces a new fast neutron measurement, fast neutron cross section (FNXS) that is highly sensitive to CO2 and gas volume
while insensitive to water salinity and volume. A special pulse sequence used with the neutron generator allows borehole effects
to be determined allowing formation capture cross section (SIGM) and neutron porosity (TPHI) to be self-compensated. Therefore,
monitoring passes can be meaningfully compared, even with changing borehole fluids and any change to the completion tubulars.


CCS1 was drilled to a depth of 7,235 ft. and completed as follows:
        Bit size of 26 inches (in.) to a depth of 355 ft., 17.5 in. to 5,339 ft., and 12.25 in to a total depth of 7,235 ft.
       Intermediate casing was 13.375 in., J-55 59.5 & 66.2 pounds per foot (lb/ft) from surface to 5,339 ft.
      The final section casing is 9.625 in. from surface to total depth with N80 40 lb/ft from surface to 5,272 ft. and 13Cr80 47
            lb/ft from 5,272 ft. to 7,219 ft.
      The injection tubing string is 4.5 in. 12.6 lb/ft from surface to 6,414 ft with the packer set at 6,365 ft.


Technical Background
Pulsed neutron Sigma (∑) is the thermal neutron capture cross section or the rate at which thermal neutrons are captured by the
formation matrix and fluids. PNX has a pulsed neutron generator that creates high-energy neutrons. These neutrons are slowed to
a thermal velocity through elastic and inelastic collisions with the nuclei of the environment’s elements, at which point they can be
captured. Hydrogen, with the most similar nuclei mass to the neutron, is the most effective element to slow the high energy
neutrons and chlorine is very good at capturing the thermal neutrons. Therefore, water has a capture cross section, which
depends largely on its salinity. Fresh water has a Sigma response of approximately 22 capture-units (cu) and salt saturated water
over 130 cu. CO2 has a very low ability to slow or capture neutrons and the Sigma response for CO2 is near zero. Using the

                                               Schlumberger-Private

contrast in Sigma for water and CO2 the formation water saturation (Sw) can be calculated from the Sigma measurement. The
Sigma measurement is corrected for the borehole environment and therefore is only sensitive to formation fluid changes.


SIBH is the rate at which thermal neutrons are captured as measured with the earlier timing gates and shorter source-detector
spacing making it primarily sensitive to the borehole, and therefore borehole and annular CO2. CO2 in the wellbore or well annuli
will decrease SIBH.


The PNX neutron porosity measurement (TPHI) is an inverse relationship of the slowing down length of high energy neutrons
emitted by the tool and responds primarily to the amount of hydrogen within the formation. Hydrogen is generally related to the
fluids in the porosity (e.g., either water or oil). The carbon and oxygen nuclei of CO2 have a much higher mass than a neutron and
interactions with high energy neutrons are primarily elastic with the neutron losing very little energy similar to other formation
elements. As CO2 saturation increases replacing formation water, the hydrogen density decreases causing the neutron porosity
measurement to be lower than the true porosity. The PNX neutron porosity has a depth of investigation around 10 to 12 inches.
The PNX TPHI algorithm uses count ratios from the three detectors and several timing gates to correct for the borehole
environment. However, CO2 in the well annuli requires a large correction. In a large borehole, the algorithm may not be able to
fully correct for the CO2. Therefore, TPHI is primarily sensitive to CO2 in the formation, lowering the measured neutron porosity.
And in large boreholes filled with CO2, the TPHI measurement may not fully correct for the environmental, effecting the
measurements accuracy.


Gas ratio (GRAT) and Fast Neutron Cross Section (FNXS) are new measurements unique to the PNX tool and based on the
measurement of gamma rays resulting from inelastic neutron interactions, which are very sensitive to CO2 and gas. Since
inelastic gamma rays can only be induced by neutrons with energies at MeV levels, they respond to formation properties that are
independent of neutron porosity and Sigma. The PNX neutron generator (minitron) burst contains a high flux of high energy
neutrons with any source variations measured and normalized using a compact neutron monitor (CNM) detector placed near the
minitron. The gamma rays resulting from the high energy neutron interactions during the minitron burst contain inelastic,
epithermal, and thermal capture events. By measuring the gamma ray events during and following a burst, the capture
background can be determined and removed from the total measured gamma rays.


GRAT is defined as the capture background corrected burst gamma ray count rate normalized by the neutron monitor count rate.
GRAT will increase in the presence CO2 and/or gas either in the formation, annulus, or in the wellbore. Characterizing GRAT for
various formation conditions was done to obtain the new measurement called fast neutron elastic scattering cross-section, FNXS.
GRAT and FNXS are independent to SIGM and TPHI, and highly sensitive to CO2 with very little sensitivity to water salinity or
formation properties. FNXS varies linearly, decreasing in the presence of CO2 and/or gas and can be used as an independent
input to calculate the saturation of CO2 and/or gas. David Rose et al. (2015) describes the PNX tool measurements in detail in
their paper titled “An Innovative Slim Pulsed Neutron Logging Tool”.


GRAT and FNXS are shallow reading measurements – two to four inches. The PNX log is centralized in the CCS1 well by the
completion to a depth of 6,414 ft. This makes GRAT and FNXS measurements primarily sensitive to the borehole and annular
space in this well with less sensitivity to the formation. In CCS1 above 6,414 ft. GRAT and FNXS cannot be used as an input to
formation fluid analysis but remain very valuable well integrity measurements. Below 6,414 ft., the GRAT and FNXS
measurements will be sensitive to the formation CO2 in addition to the annular space. Where there is CO2 in the borehole below
6,414 ft. effecting the accuracy of TPHI, FNXS can be used as an input for formation CO2 saturation evaluation.

interval and 1.16 g/cm3 brine below, presumably with dissolved CO2. The post injection water – CO2 interface below the
perforations moved from 7,049 ft. during injection to around 7,033 ft in October 2016 and 7,026 ft in May 2018 and March 2019.


Inspection of the PNX time-lapse measurements sensitive to borehole and annular space are used to evaluate well integrity and
detect CO2 in the annular space or formations outside of the injection zone. Some of the measurements sensitive to the annular
space are Sigma borehole (SIBH), and Fast Neutron elastic scattering Cross-Section (FNXS), and Thermal Neutron Porosity
(TPHI), all decreasing with the presence of CO2.


TPHI and FNXS measurements are corrected for the borehole environment. In the single casing portion of the well below the
tubing shoe at 6,414 ft., TPHI and FNXS are primarily sensitive to formation CO2 and can be partially corrected for the annular
space. SIBH is more sensitive to the borehole environment and has a correction for the formation. In order to detect possible
annular CO2, other raw or uncorrected measurements like Sigma Short Spacing Near Apparent (SSNA) and capture background
corrected burst gamma ray (GRAT) are also inspected.


Figure 1 shows the PNX time-lapse inspection log for the depth range 6,660 to 7,124 ft and Figure 2 for the depth range 6,300 to
6,725 ft. Time-lapse PNX measurements, SIBH, FNXS and TPHI in July 2014 show CO2 in the borehole to the bottom of the
perforated interval at 7,049 ft. with a transition to water around 7,083 ft. CO2 injection stopped in November 2014 and the October
2016 time-lapse PNX measurements show the CO2 - water contact had move up to around 7,033 ft. and to 7,026 ft in May 2018
and March 2019 with a shorter transition zone to borehole water below the perforated interval. Some CO2 is detected in the
interval 6,828 to 6,830 ft. and indication of possible CO2 up to 6,648 ft. There is no detectable CO2 above 6,648 ft. to the tubing
shoe at 6,414 ft.


The PNX is centered in the wellbore by the tubing above 6,414 ft. SIBH remains sensitive to the borehole and annular spaces.
FNXS is more sensitive to the annular spaces and less to the formation due to its shallow depth of investigation. TPHI is primarily
sensitive to the formation up to 5,339 ft. Above 5,339 ft. the wellbore bit size was 17.5 in. and TPHI loses much of its sensitivity to
the formation. Inspection of the PNX time-lapse measurements SIBH, TPHI and FNXS show no detected CO2 in the wellbore
annulus in the tubing section of CCS1.


Figure 3 shows the PNX time-lapse inspection log for the depth range 4,560 to 6,300 ft. The time-lapse measurements SIBH,
FNXS and TPHI repeat very well for the Oct 2016, May 2018 and March 2019 logs. There are some differences in the July 2014

There are four depths with large increases in FNXS indicating a change or additional hardware in the completion. These depths
are 4,461, 5,588, 6,140 and 6,326 ft. The increase at 6,326 indicates the position of the Pressure Temperature Gauge Mandrel
and the other three are the positions of the monitoring Geophones.

CO2 saturations around the injection zone remained mostly constant during the nearly two-year period post CO2 injection,
November 2014 to October 2016. There are three main differences observed in the October 2016 log. 1) There are some free-
phase CO2 buoyancy effects with the bottom depth of CO2 saturation for all zones listed above moving upwards a few feet above
apart from 6,969 – 6,977 ft. with no change. 2) A small amount of CO2 is observed in Oct 2016 above the injection zones up to
6,915 ft. 3) The October 2016 log shows an influx of formation water between the lower two perforations in the interval 7,021 to
7,006 ft indicated by the increase in the SIGM, TPHI and FNXS measurements in this zone into the near wellbore.


The May 2018 interpretation showed a significant drop in the CO2 saturation in the Lower Mt Simon around the injection interval
from the October 2016 log. The maximum CO2 saturation in the interval 6,940 – 7,050 ft was 56% in October 2016 and had
dropped to 31% by May 2018. The CO2 saturation average was 29% in October 2016 and had dropped to 11% by May 2018.
These CO2 saturations are similar to those observed in the VW1 observation well during the injection period. High CO2 saturations
concentrated near the injection well may have remained until CO2 saturations further from the well had time to diffuse to a more
uniform level in the Lower Mt Simon. The March 2019 PNX survey showed the CO2 saturation near the injection interval to remain
about the same as the May 2018 survey. The main difference being the interval increased in height. The May 2018 interpretation
shows the majority of the CO2 in the interval 6,940 – 7,035 ft and a small amount at 6,920 – 6,924 ft. The March 2019
interpretation shows the lower interval expanded 5 ft. to 6,940 – 7,040 ft and the upper interval expanded 16 ft. to 6,904 – 6,924 ft.


The May 2018 PNX log shows a new interval in the Upper Mt Simon A, 6,840 to 6,830 ft. with CO2. This interval had a maximum
CO2 saturation of 30% and average of 19%. The nearby IL-ICCS project is injecting CO2 into the Upper Mt. Simon A and Mt
Simon B formations, so this new CO2 is likely a result of the IL-ICCS CO2 storage. The IL-ICCS project began CO2 injection in the
Upper Mt Simon A and Mt Simon B formation on April 7, 2017 and had injected 687,440 tonnes at the time of the May 2018 CCS1
log. The March 2019 PNX log shows an increase in CO2 in this same Upper Mt Simon A interval. The CO2 saturation increased
from a maximum of 30% in 2018 to 44% and the average from 19% to 26%. The total injection volume was 1,094,643 tonnes at
the time of the March 2019 PNX survey.


The May 2018 and March 2019 PNX interpretations indicate small amounts of CO2 in the Mt Simon Upper A and lower portion of
Mt Simon B formations up to 6,650 ft., above the 6,840 to 6,830 ft. zone discussed in the previous paragraph. This interval of the
Mt. Simon A and Mt Simon B has some fresher fluid remaining in the near wellbore from the 2011 well completion. During well
construction, drilling mud filtrate which was much lower in salinity than the formation water invaded the near wellbore formation.
Sigma has a depth of investigation of around 10 to 12 inches, so in intervals with drilling mud invasion the measurement will
contain both formation and drilling mud filtrate waters. Fresher fluids remaining in the near wellbore is determined from the
response of Sigma, TPHI and FNXS. TPHI and FNXS measurements have very low sensitivity to the salinity compared to CO2,
and they indicate the formation fluid is water. Sigma is too low for this water to be native formation water salinity. Also, Sigma is
continuing to increase as the near wellbore invaded water diffuses and is replaced by native formation water. This Sigma increase
is most evident in the interval 6,780 to 6,815 ft. where most of the non-native near wellbore fluid has diffused. TPHI and FNXS
measurements show almost no change indicating only a salinity change has occurred causing Sigma to increase. The
interpretation challenge with Sigma increasing from a salinity change is detecting a small amount of CO2 which may only suppress
the increase. In this case, formation CO2 saturation is largely dependent on the TPHI and FNXS measurements. An additional
complication is the CO2 filled borehole. For a CO2 filled borehole, TPHI and FNXS have large corrections which adds some
uncertainty. In the interval 6,830 to 6,650 ft., the small amount of formation CO2 calculated is close to the uncertainty of TPHI and

Previous fluid interpretations prior to Dec 2014 using RST data indicated small amounts of CO2 in the upper Mt. Simon A which is
believed to be erroneous, particularly for the depth interval 6,707 to 6,813 ft. This CO2 is not present in interpretations using the
newer PNX log data. The RST Pulsed Neutron Log interpretations used Sigma PHIC neutron porosity which has much more
uncertainty than the self-correcting algorithms of the PNX. The PNX’s neutron porosity, TPHI, has better precision and accuracy
and does not give the erroneously interpreted CO2, while maintaining sensitivity to saturation changes. In addition to a more
precise and accurate neutron porosity compared to the RST, PNX has the new FNXS measurement which is sensitive to CO2 and
very little sensitivity to water salinity. FNXS varies linearly with CO2 volume and can be used as an additional input to solve for
CO2 saturation. FNXS was used for the July 2014, October 2016, May 2018 and March 2019 PNX logs to evaluate the formation
fluids.


Most of drilling mud filtrate in the lower Mt. Simon A is believed to be diffused or displaced by the CO2 injection leaving only
formation water and CO2 as possible pore fluids. Any CO2 present would decrease Sigma and the neutron porosity with both
measurements reinforcing each other in the interpretation. As a result, the RST CO2 saturation in the lower Mt. Simon A has a
higher confidence than zones that have diffusing drilling mud filtrate. The confidence in the PNX interpretations using FNXS does
not change for the zones with and without diffusing drilling mud filtrate.

3.  Conclusions


A Pulsed Neutron eXtreme (PNX) log was run to evaluate well integrity and formation CO2 saturation in the CCS1 well on March 6,
2018. Measurements sensitive to annular CO2 were inspected and compared to previous well integrity logs. The Illinois Basin –
Decatur Project injected approximately one million tonnes of CO2 through perforations in the CCS1 well into the lower Mt. Simon A
over a three-year period from November 17, 2011 to November 26, 2014. Pulsed Neutron Log (PNL) monitoring during the
injection period showed the majority of the CO2 to be contained in the lower Mt Simon A interval 6,940 – 7,050 ft. with a small
amount extending up into the bottom of the Upper Mt Simon A to 6,912 ft. CO2 saturations remained fairly constant throughout the
injection period with CO2 segmented into the permeable formation layers. The average CO2 saturation in the interval 6,940 –
7,050 ft. averaged 29% with a maximum saturation of 56%.. Post injection PNL monitoring in October 2016 showed very little
change in CO2 saturations apart from some buoyancy effects reducing CO2 saturations at the bottom of the permeable zones, and
the average CO2 saturations remaining constant.


The May 2018 PNX monitoring log showed a significant reduction of the CO2 saturation with average CO2 saturation in the interval
6,940 – 7,050 ft. dropping from 29% to11% and maximum from 56% to 31%. This CO2 saturation level is closer to PNL measured
saturations at the VW1 observation well during the injection period. This may indicate high CO2 saturations concentrated near the
injection well may have remained until CO2 saturations further from the well had time to diffuse to a more uniform level in the
Lower Mt Simon. The March 2019 log interpretation showed similar CO2 saturations near the injection interval although with some
increase in height. The May 2018 interpretation shows the majority of the CO2 in the interval 6,940 – 7,035 ft and a small amount
at 6,920 – 6,924 ft. The March 2019 interpretation shows the lower interval expanded 5 ft. to 6,940 – 7,040 ft and the upper
interval expanded 16 ft. to 6,904 – 6,924 ft.


The May 2018 PNX log showed a new interval with CO2 in the Upper Mt Simon A at 6,840 to 6,830 ft. The IL-ICCS project began
CO2 injection in the Upper Mt Simon A and Mt Simon B formation on April 7, 2017 and had injected 687,440 tonnes at the time of
the May 2018 CCS1 log. The CO2 detected in the May 2018 PNX survey at 6,840 to 6,830 ft. is likely a result of the IL-ICCS CO2
storage. The March 2019 PNX log shows an increase in CO2 in this same Upper Mt Simon A interval. The CO2 saturation
increased from a maximum of 30% in 2018 to 44% in 2019 and the average from 19% to 26%. The total injection volume was
1,094,643 tonnes at the time of the March 2019 PNX survey.


The May 2018 and March 2019 PNX interpretations indicate small amounts of CO2 in the Mt Simon Upper A and lower portion of
Mt Simon B formations up to 6,650 ft., above the 6,840 to 6,830 ft. zone discussed in the previous paragraph. Most of the interval
above 6,830 ft to 6,650 ft. still has water in the near wellbore with lower salinity than the formation water. This lower salinity water
comes from the well construction and continues to diffuse with time and being replaced with native formation water. The diffusion
of the non-native water causes Sigma to increase and countering any decrease from small amounts of CO2. In this case,
formation CO2 saturation computation is largely dependent on the TPHI and FNXS measurements. An additional complication is
the CO2 filled borehole. For a CO2 filled borehole, TPHI and FNXS have large corrections which adds some uncertainty. The CO2
calculated above 6,830 to 6,650 ft. is within the uncertainty of the measurements and below the threshold of definite detection.


The March 2019 PNX survey indicates no change to annular fluids in either the casing to formation or tubing to casing annuli were
detected above 6,650 ft. The PNX mechanical integrity log indicates CO2 is contained within the tubing and casing of the borehole
and in areas of the reservoir where expected. There is nothing in the data to indicate that the mechanical integrity of the well has
been compromised.
